screens.title: Boolean Expressions and Comparison Operators
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how programs make decisions by using Boolean expressions that evaluate to True or False. A Boolean value is a special type with only two possible values: True and False. You will see how comparison operators like equals, not equals, less than, and greater than produce Boolean results, and how logical operators — and, or, not — combine those results to express more complex conditions. We will practice common examples you already know, such as checking whether someone is old enough, whether a password matches, and guarding a division so we avoid a division-by-zero. You will also learn about short-circuit evaluation, which can change whether parts of a condition run at all, and truthiness, where numbers, strings, and collections act like Booleans in conditions. By the end you'll be able to write clear conditions, store them in well-named variables, and avoid common mistakes like using a single equals for assignment or comparing floats for exact equality. Think about a real question you want a program to answer — your code will express that as a Boolean.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what Boolean values are and why they are useful, use comparison operators to write conditions, combine conditions with logical operators, and evaluate the truth of complex expressions. First, you will learn that Python provides a bool type with two keywords: True and False. Knowing this means you can name conditions explicitly and avoid treating them as strings. Second, you will practice each comparison operator — equality, inequality, less-than, greater-than, and their or-equal forms — and see concrete examples like 5 equals 5 or 5 greater than 3. Third, you will combine conditions with and, or, and not to express compound questions, for example checking age and possession of a permit. Finally, you will evaluate expressions step by step, including how short-circuit evaluation can stop parts of an expression from running. These skills let you write safe checks, avoid runtime errors, and make your program logic readable. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the rule and a verified competency milestone to guide practice.

screens.title: What is a Boolean value?
screens.narratorSegment: A Boolean value is the simplest data type for decision-making: it answers a single question with either True or False. In Python the bool type has exactly two keywords, True and False, and they are not strings or numbers. When you assign is_valid = True, you are storing a Boolean that other expressions and statements can evaluate. This is useful because it gives meaning to conditions: a variable named is_adult stores whether a person meets an age rule, and code reads clearly when you use descriptive names. A common beginner confusion is to treat True and False like text. Remember the capitalization: Python requires True and False with leading capital letters. Another misconception is thinking Boolean values can represent multiple states; they only represent two possibilities. For clarity, prefer explicit checks when you care about a specific value — for example, testing name!= "" rather than relying on truthiness — until you are comfortable with how Python interprets non-Boolean values as True or False. Practically, booleans are the gatekeepers of control flow: if a condition evaluates to True, a branch runs; otherwise it does not. Try naming your Boolean variables so their meaning reads like a question, such as has_ticket or can_enter, because that makes conditionals easier to read and debug.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Boolean value
Definition

The bool type and its meaning

A Boolean answers a single yes/no question and stores True or False. Naming matters for readability.

Code example
is_valid = True
has_error = False
print(type(is_valid))  # <class 'bool'>
Example
Use is_adult = age >= 18 to store a condition and reuse it in multiple checks.
Common misconception
Treating True as a string or expecting more than two Boolean states — a Boolean is strictly True or False.
Key Takeaway

Booleans are explicit truth values. Name them as questions to make conditionals readable and robust.

Analogy

Light switch analogy

Think of True as a light turned on and False as off. A Boolean answers a single yes/no question for your program.

Try this
Create variables named has_ticket or can_enter so your if statements read like plain English.
Check your understanding
Why prefer is_adult = age >= 18 over directly writing age >= 18 in many places? Answer: naming improves clarity and avoids repeating logic.

screens.title: Comparison Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison operators compare two values and yield a Boolean result. The most used ones are equality (double equals) and inequality, plus the relational operators for order. A direct example: 5 == 5 evaluates to True while 5 = when inclusive bounds are needed, for example age >= 18 for adult checks. The lesson content includes a table of operator meanings and results; practice by predicting the result of each comparison before running code. Keep comparisons simple and explicit to avoid confusion, and when checking user input normalize types first — for example convert input to an integer before comparing to a number. Predicting results before running code trains your mental model and helps you spot mistakes quickly. Comparison Operators means use comparison operators to test relationships between values; remember assignment vs comparison.. In practical terms, ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= produce boolean results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Comparison Operators
Operators

Meaning and examples

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
==Equal to5 == 5True
!=Not equal to5 != 3True
<Less than5 < 3False
>Greater than5 > 3True
<=Less than or equal5 <= 5True
>=Greater than or equal5 >= 6False
Tip
Always ensure the operands are comparable types. Convert user input into numbers before numeric comparisons.
Key Takeaway

Comparison operators return Boolean results. Predict results before running code to verify understanding.

Common mistakes

Assignment vs Comparison and floats

Assignment vs comparison
Remember: x = 5 assigns. x == 5 compares. Using = in a condition causes a syntax error in Python.
Floating-point equality
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to False due to floating-point imprecision. Use a small epsilon check like abs(a - b) < 0.0001 when needed.
Quick example
abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 0.0001  # True when treated with epsilon

screens.title: Logical Operators: and, or, not
screens.narratorSegment: Logical operators let you combine comparisons into more expressive conditions. The and operator returns True only when both sides are True. The or operator returns True when at least one side is True. The not operator flips a Boolean value. These operators let you write checks like age >= 18 and has_id to require two facts simultaneously, or is_weekend or is_holiday to allow either condition. A practical habit is writing expressions that read like English sentences. A misconception is thinking and and or evaluate both sides always; Python short-circuits, which we will examine on the next screen. For now, practice by reading and tracing the code: imagine each comparison as True or False and apply operator rules step by step. Here is a short code walkthrough that shows common patterns: check age and id, use or for alternate permissions, and not to invert conditions. When you store a Boolean result in a variable, you can reuse a clear name like can_enter in multiple places. Also, bear in mind operator precedence: not runs before and/or, and parentheses can enforce the intended order. Try mental evaluation of each line before running the code to strengthen your understanding.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Logical Operators
Code walkthrough

and, or, not with examples

age = 25
has_id = True
print(age >= 18 and has_id)  # True

is_weekend = True
is_holiday = False
print(is_weekend or is_holiday)  # True

is_raining = False
print(not is_raining)  # True
Why it matters
Compound conditions let you capture real-world business logic compactly and avoid nested if statements.
Misconception
Don't assume both sides always run. Short-circuiting can skip evaluation of the second expression in many cases.
Key Takeaway

Use logical operators to combine conditions clearly, and rely on parentheses to make precedence explicit.

Analogy

Gates and switches

Think of and as a gate that needs both green lights, or as a gate that accepts any green light, and not as a flip that turns green to red and vice versa.

Check your understanding
What is the result of True and (False or True)? Answer: True. Evaluate inner parentheses first.

screens.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation
screens.narratorSegment: Short-circuit evaluation is how Python saves work and avoids errors by not evaluating parts of an expression that are unnecessary to decide the final result. For an and expression, if the first operand is False, Python already knows the whole expression will be False and it doesn't evaluate the second operand. For an or expression, if the first operand is True, Python knows the whole expression will be True and skips the second part. This behavior is useful and sometimes essential. For example, you can safely check a divisor before dividing: if divisor!= 0 and dividend / divisor > 2: then the division only runs when the divisor check passes, preventing a runtime error. A common misconception is thinking both sides always run, which can lead to surprises when the right-hand side has a function call or side effect. When reading code, notice that short-circuiting can be used intentionally to avoid work, but it can also hide bugs if the author relied on the skipped expression to perform an important action. When in doubt, write the safety check first or use explicit conditionals.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Short-Circuit Evaluation
Concept

Short-circuit evaluation explained

and short-circuit
If the left expression is False, the right expression is not evaluated because the whole and is False.
or short-circuit
If the left expression is True, the right expression is not evaluated because the whole or is True.
Practical pattern
# Only divide if divisor is not zero
if divisor != 0 and dividend / divisor > 2:
    print("Result is greater than 2")
In this pattern the division is safe because the divisor check runs first and prevents division by zero.
Misuse risk
If the skipped expression had side effects, those side effects won't occur. Avoid relying on side effects inside conditions.
Pro tip
Place safety checks first when using and to guarantee safe evaluation of later expressions.

screens.title: Truthiness of Non-Boolean Values
screens.narratorSegment: Python treats many non-Boolean values as either truthy or falsy when used in a Boolean context such as an if statement. The chapter lists familiar rules: the number 0 is treated as False while any non-zero number is True. An empty string is False while any non-empty string is True. Empty collections like [] or {} are False and non-empty collections are True. None is always False. These rules are convenient for quick checks but can confuse beginners. For readability and correctness, especially when learning, prefer explicit comparisons. For example, instead of if name: you may prefer if name!= "" until you are confident about truthiness. A concrete example from the lesson shows name = "" then if name prints a message that the name is empty. A misconception is assuming that all falsy values compare equal; they do not. False, 0, "", and None are distinct values even if they act like False in conditions. Use explicit checks when your code must distinguish between these cases. Practicing with print(bool(value)) for different values helps build an accurate mental model quickly.

keyIdea.title: Truthiness rules
keyIdea.text: 0, empty strings, empty collections, and None are falsy; non-empty values and non-zero numbers are truthy. Use explicit checks if you need to distinguish values.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Truthiness
Concept

When non-Boolean values act like True or False

Numbers
0 is False; any other number is True. Use bool(value) to check.
Strings
Empty string "" is False; non-empty strings are True.
Collections
Empty lists, tuples, sets, and dicts are False; non-empty are True.
None
None is always False in Boolean contexts.
Example
name = ""
if name:
    print("Name is provided")
else:
    print("Name is empty")
# Output: Name is empty
Key Takeaway

Truthiness is convenient but can hide distinctions. Use explicit checks for clarity when you need to differentiate values.

Practice

Try bool() on these values

0, 1, "", "hello", None — check each with the bool constructor to see how Python evaluates them.
Hands-on hint
Print bool(0) and bool("") to confirm they are False, and bool(1) and bool("hello") to confirm they are True.

screens.title: Floating-Point Comparison and Epsilon
screens.narratorSegment: Floating-point arithmetic sometimes produces unexpected results because binary representations can't exactly express some decimal fractions. The chapter gives a classic example: 0.1 plus 0.2 does not equal 0.3 exactly in floating-point, so the equality comparison returns False. For beginners this can be surprising, but the safe response is simple: compare with a small tolerance or epsilon. The common pattern is to check whether the absolute difference between two numbers is smaller than a chosen small value, for example abs(a - b) < 0.0001. That treats two nearly equal values as equal for practical purposes. A misconception is to assume exact equality always holds for decimals; instead, think in terms of approximations when dealing with floats. When your logic depends on exact decimal arithmetic, consider using decimals or integers representing cents, but for now, the epsilon comparison is the recommended beginner technique. Practice by computing the sum and printing both the raw float and the epsilon comparison so you see the small difference that causes the direct equality to fail. Floating-Point Comparison and Epsilon means avoid direct float equality; use an epsilon comparison like abs(a - b) < small_value for safe checks.. In practical terms, why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 can be false and how to compare safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Floating-point comparison
Issue

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 may be False

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  # Often False
print(0.1 + 0.2)          # Shows small rounding difference

# Use epsilon to compare
abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 0.0001  # True if difference is tiny
Why it matters
In equality checks, floating-point representation can mislead comparisons. Using epsilon avoids brittle conditions.
Key Takeaway

Treat float equality as approximate. Use an absolute difference check when exact equality is not reliable.

Example walkthrough
Run the code that prints the raw sum and the epsilon result. Observe that while direct equality may fail, the epsilon comparison recognizes near equality in practice.
Practice
Try different epsilon values to understand sensitivity. Larger epsilon tolerates bigger differences but may hide real errors.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Expression Evaluation
Worked example

5 > 3 and (2 < 1 or 4 == 4) and not False

Step 1: Parentheses
2 < 1 is False. 4 == 4 is True. False or True → True.
Step 2: not
not False → True.
Step 3: Remaining and
5 > 3 → True. True and True and True → True. Final result is True.
Why this helps
Breaking complex expressions into small steps makes it easy to follow operator precedence and to spot where short-circuiting might skip evaluation in other examples.
Common misconception
Assuming and/or have equal precedence; use parentheses or stepwise evaluation to be sure.
Try this
Change one part of the expression to False and re-evaluate the steps to see where short-circuiting would kick in.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how programs make decisions by using Boolean expressions that evaluate to True or False. A Boolean value is a special type with only two possible values: True and False. You will see how comparison operators like equals, not equals, less than, and greater than produce Boolean results, and how logical operators — and, or, not — combine those results to express more complex conditions. We will practice common examples you already know, such as checking whether someone is old enough, whether a password matches, and guarding a division so we avoid a division-by-zero. You will also learn about short-circuit evaluation, which can change whether parts of a condition run at all, and truthiness, where numbers, strings, and collections act like Booleans in conditions. By the end you'll be able to write clear conditions, store them in well-named variables, and avoid common mistakes like using a single equals for assignment or comparing floats for exact equality. Think about a real question you want a program to answer — your code will express that as a Boolean.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what Boolean values are and why they are useful, use comparison operators to write conditions, combine conditions with logical operators, and evaluate the truth of complex expressions. First, you will learn that Python provides a bool type with two keywords: True and False. Knowing this means you can name conditions explicitly and avoid treating them as strings. Second, you will practice each comparison operator — equality, inequality, less-than, greater-than, and their or-equal forms — and see concrete examples like 5 equals 5 or 5 greater than 3. Third, you will combine conditions with and, or, and not to express compound questions, for example checking age and possession of a permit. Finally, you will evaluate expressions step by step, including how short-circuit evaluation can stop parts of an expression from running. These skills let you write safe checks, avoid runtime errors, and make your program logic readable. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the rule and a verified competency milestone to guide practice.

These practice targets map to the chapter exercises you will run. First, practice declaring Boolean variables and printing their type so you can recognize the bool type. Second, practice each comparison operator with simple numeric examples — equality and inequality plus greater-than and less-than. Third, form compound conditions with and, or, and not, and test them with simple values such as age and a permit flag. Fourth, try truthiness checks with zero, empty string, and None so you can spot when a value will behave like False. Each skill has a milestone: write a short script that asks for age, computes an is_adult Boolean, asks about a permit, and prints whether the user can legally drive. This single script verifies multiple objectives at once, and it also highlights important mistakes like using assignment instead of comparison or relying on exact float equality. Working through these small, targeted practices builds confidence before you apply these checks in larger programs.

A Boolean value is the simplest data type for decision-making: it answers a single question with either True or False. In Python the bool type has exactly two keywords, True and False, and they are not strings or numbers. When you assign is_valid = True, you are storing a Boolean that other expressions and statements can evaluate. This is useful because it gives meaning to conditions: a variable named is_adult stores whether a person meets an age rule, and code reads clearly when you use descriptive names. A common beginner confusion is to treat True and False like text. Remember the capitalization: Python requires True and False with leading capital letters. Another misconception is thinking Boolean values can represent multiple states; they only represent two possibilities. For clarity, prefer explicit checks when you care about a specific value — for example, testing name!= "" rather than relying on truthiness — until you are comfortable with how Python interprets non-Boolean values as True or False. Practically, booleans are the gatekeepers of control flow: if a condition evaluates to True, a branch runs; otherwise it does not. Try naming your Boolean variables so their meaning reads like a question, such as has_ticket or can_enter, because that makes conditionals easier to read and debug.

Comparison operators compare two values and yield a Boolean result. The most used ones are equality (double equals) and inequality, plus the relational operators for order. A direct example: 5 == 5 evaluates to True while 5 = when inclusive bounds are needed, for example age >= 18 for adult checks. The lesson content includes a table of operator meanings and results; practice by predicting the result of each comparison before running code. Keep comparisons simple and explicit to avoid confusion, and when checking user input normalize types first — for example convert input to an integer before comparing to a number. Predicting results before running code trains your mental model and helps you spot mistakes quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Logical operators let you combine comparisons into more expressive conditions. The and operator returns True only when both sides are True. The or operator returns True when at least one side is True. The not operator flips a Boolean value. These operators let you write checks like age >= 18 and has_id to require two facts simultaneously, or is_weekend or is_holiday to allow either condition. A practical habit is writing expressions that read like English sentences. A misconception is thinking and and or evaluate both sides always; Python short-circuits, which we will examine on the next screen. For now, practice by reading and tracing the code: imagine each comparison as True or False and apply operator rules step by step. Here is a short code walkthrough that shows common patterns: check age and id, use or for alternate permissions, and not to invert conditions. When you store a Boolean result in a variable, you can reuse a clear name like can_enter in multiple places. Also, bear in mind operator precedence: not runs before and/or, and parentheses can enforce the intended order. Try mental evaluation of each line before running the code to strengthen your understanding.

Short-circuit evaluation is how Python saves work and avoids errors by not evaluating parts of an expression that are unnecessary to decide the final result. For an and expression, if the first operand is False, Python already knows the whole expression will be False and it doesn't evaluate the second operand. For an or expression, if the first operand is True, Python knows the whole expression will be True and skips the second part. This behavior is useful and sometimes essential. For example, you can safely check a divisor before dividing: if divisor!= 0 and dividend / divisor > 2: then the division only runs when the divisor check passes, preventing a runtime error. A common misconception is thinking both sides always run, which can lead to surprises when the right-hand side has a function call or side effect. When reading code, notice that short-circuiting can be used intentionally to avoid work, but it can also hide bugs if the author relied on the skipped expression to perform an important action. When in doubt, write the safety check first or use explicit conditionals.

Python treats many non-Boolean values as either truthy or falsy when used in a Boolean context such as an if statement.
